title: “Do You Know What Birth Control Actually Does to Your Body?”: Assessing Contraceptive Information on TikTok
screen_reason: QUALITY-ONLY study. The 100 TikTok contraception videos were appraised with the DISCERN instrument (reliability / quality / overall-quality subscales) and reported as MEDIAN SCALE SCORES (DISCERN-T median 27, min-max 24-30.5), never as a share of videos judged false, misleading or inaccurate against any external ground truth. No item was coded true/false; no fact-check, guideline-concordance or source-reliability list was applied. Per §3, DISCERN scores map to construct QUALITY, and per §3 a rating scale reported only as a central-tendency score is not a share, so no row is created. The other percentages the paper reports (53% of videos rejected hormonal birth control; 34% expressed distrust in health professionals and/or hormonal contraception; 38% discussed fertility awareness/cycle tracking; 10% of creators were medical professionals) are content-topic/stance categories, not veracity judgements — a wholly accurate video can fall in every one of them.
missed_or_uncertain: Deliberately NOT extracted, with reasons: (1) DISCERN-T median 27 (min-max 24-30.5), DISCERN-R median 14 (12-16), DISCERN-Q median 11 (9.5-13), DISCERN-OQ median 2 (2-2.5) — scale scores, not shares; §3 says a scale reported only as a mean/median yields no row. If the review does want QUALITY scale rows, DISCERN-T median 27/80 is the number to use (n = 100 videos; by creator group: general uploader 26.25, hormone health coach 26, health educator 27.5, online company 29, medical professional 33). (2) '53% of the creators ... explicitly rejected hormonal birth control' and '34% of all video creators expressed distrust in health professional advice and/or hormonal contraception' — stance/attitude categories, not falsity, so not CONTENT under the §3 QUALITY-vs-CONTENT test. (3) 'Five videos discussed some alternative measures of birth control, including the use of papaya seeds, coconut oil, and neem oil as natural spermicides' (5/100) — this is the closest the paper comes to a countable false-content claim (these are not evidence-based contraceptives), but the authors never code those five videos as inaccurate or misinformation; coding 5% here would be my inference, not the paper's, so it is not extracted. ADJUDICATOR NOTE: the paper's abstract asserts 'a prominent presence of contraceptive health misinformation' purely as an inference from low DISCERN scores; a first extractor could plausibly have created a row from that framing, but it is not backed by any numerator of false items.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis. TikTok searched Aug-Sep 2023 from a newly opened account simulating an 18-year-old female user in Australia (to blunt personalisation); 33 candidate hashtags reduced to 5 (#birthcontrol, #contraception, #thepill, #naturalbirthcontrol, #cycletracking) above a 75-million-view cutoff; top 25 videos per hashtag retrieved, top 20 retained after exclusions (duplicates, off-topic, non-English, deleted), n = 100. Two non-clinical public-health reviewers (AD, MB) independently extracted characteristics and independently rated the 16 DISCERN items; a third reviewer with clinical expertise (CM) adjudicated discrepancies. Reported reliability (pre-adjudication, quadratic weighted Cohen's kappa): 0.62 reliability items, 0.51 quality items, 0.46 overall quality. Analysis in STATA; Kruskal-Wallis with Bonferroni post hoc across creator groups. Author-stated limitations: subjective hashtag selection, n = 100, English-only, single time point, DISCERN not validated for short-form video, possible creator-categorisation error.
rob.item6_quote: Given that the intent behind messages is often unclear, whether created by genuinely concerned individuals or those undermining trust in healthcare, the term “misinformation” will be used hereafter for all false or misleading health-​related information [17].
rob.item10_quote: From the remaining videos for each of the five hashtags, only the top 20 videos were chosen to ensure an even distribution across the hashtags, totalling 100 videos for data analysis (see Figure 1).
